ssc.label: No SSC
ssc.definition: Dead start or paused. No elastic contribution; force comes from rate of development alone.

ssc.label: Slow SSC
ssc.definition: Contact > 250 ms, large joint displacement. Countermovement assists the jump.

ssc.label: Fast SSC
ssc.definition: Contact < 250 ms, small displacement. Trains tendon stiffness and reactive strength.

ssc.label: Eccentric only
ssc.definition: Deceleration and landing. No concentric phase to train.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

exercises.name: Back Squat
synergists: adductor magnus (strong hip extensor at depth)
exercises.position: Hip and knee flex together, so the biarticular rectus femoris stays near-constant in length and contributes little — growth and strength land on the monoarticular vasti. Adductor magnus is a major hip extensor out of the hole and is routinely mis-filed as a groin muscle.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Hardest just above the bottom position.
cues: Brace before you unrack, not after
Knees track over the mid-foot
Depth you can own without the pelvis tucking

exercises.name: Front Squat
exercises.position: Bar in front forces a more upright trunk, shortening the hip moment arm and lengthening the knee's. More quad, less hip, and far less lumbar flexion moment than a back squat at the same load — which is why it is often the first swap for a cranky lower back rather than abandoning squatting.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Fails when the trunk loses position, not when the legs do.
cues: Elbows up — the rack position is the lift
Stay vertical; let the knees travel
Ankle mobility decides your depth here

exercises.name: Pause Back Squat
stabilizers: erector spinae (very high — the hold is the demand)
exercises.position: The pause removes any elastic contribution and exposes whether position is actually owned at depth. Same muscles as a back squat, much higher demand on isometric trunk endurance.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Lighter absolute loads for the same difficulty.
cues: Still at the bottom — no sinking, no bouncing
Hold the brace through the pause
Drive without re-dipping

exercises.name: Quarter Back Squat
exercises.position: Short range allows loads well above a full squat, which is the point and also the risk: axial compression is the highest of any lift here while the muscles work through very little range.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Very heavy, very short range.
cues: Quarter depth, controlled — not a bounce
Rack height and spotters set before loading
Not a substitute for full-range work

exercises.name: Wall Sit
exercises.position: Back supported against the wall removes the spine from the equation entirely — no axial load, no flexion moment. The quad stimulus with the lowest spinal cost available, which makes it the fallback when loaded squatting is off the table.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, isometric. Time under tension is the dose.
cues: Thighs parallel to the floor
Weight in the heels, back flat on the wall
Breathe — do not brace into a Valsalva

exercises.name: Cossack Squat
exercises.position: The only frontal-plane squat here. Loads the adductors at long length on the straight leg while the bent leg does a deep single-leg squat — a combination no sagittal exercise reproduces.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or light held load. Hardest at the bottom.
cues: Keep both heels down if you can
Straight leg's toes point up
Chest up — do not round into the bottom

exercises.name: Deadlift
exercises.position: Every rep starts from a dead stop, so there is no elastic assistance. The erectors work as a prime mover here rather than a stabilizer, which is what separates it from a squat despite overlapping muscle lists.
exercises.resistance: External. Hardest off the floor and at the knee.
cues: Take the slack out before you pull
Hips and chest rise together
Reset each rep — no touch-and-go when fatigued

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift
exercises.position: Knees stay soft so the hamstrings lengthen at the hip without shortening at the knee — the opposite arrangement to a leg curl, which is why the two are not interchangeable despite both being 'hamstrings'. Peak tension is at long muscle length, near the bottom.
exercises.resistance: External. Hardest at the bottom, where the lever is longest.
cues: Push the hips back, do not bend down
Bar stays against the legs
Stop where your back position stops, not where the floor is

exercises.name: Stiff Legged Deadlift
exercises.position: Straighter knees push the hamstrings to even longer length than an RDL and lengthen the spinal lever further. The highest lumbar flexion demand in this block — the first exercise to remove for a flexion-intolerant back, and often confused with the RDL.
exercises.resistance: External. Hardest at full stretch.
cues: Knees soft but essentially straight
Range comes from the hips
Lighter than you think — this is not a max-effort lift

exercises.name: Good Morning
exercises.position: Bar on the back combines axial compression with the longest flexion lever in the block — the two lumbar stressors at once. Powerful for posterior-chain strength and the single clearest contraindication for a flexion-sensitive lower back.
exercises.resistance: External, axial, long lever. Hardest at the bottom.
cues: Hinge, do not squat down
Brace hard and keep the bar path over the feet
Stop well before the back rounds

exercises.name: Seated Good Morning
joints: trunk flexion / extension against load (isometric to concentric)
exercises.position: Sitting removes the hamstrings' contribution almost entirely, because the hip is already flexed and cannot extend. What is left is a near-pure spinal extensor exercise — a different purpose from the standing version, not a regression of it.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Demand concentrated on the erectors.
cues: Movement comes from the trunk, not the hips
Very light to start
Not a lower-back rehab exercise — it is the opposite

exercises.name: Kettlebell Swing
exercises.gct: rapid hip reversal at the bottom
exercises.position: The only ballistic hinge here — the hamstrings load fast at the bottom and the hips snap through. Trains the hinge pattern at speed without the axial load of a barbell, since the weight hangs in front rather than sitting on the spine.
exercises.resistance: External, held low and in front. Hardest at the bottom reversal.
cues: Hips snap, arms are ropes
Bell floats — do not lift it with the shoulders
Stand tall at the top, no leaning back

exercises.name: Split Squat
exercises.position: Both feet on the ground, so balance is manageable while the load still sits mostly on one leg. The entry point to all single-leg work and the cleanest place to find a left–right strength gap.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or held load. Hardest at the bottom.
cues: Torso upright, weight on the front leg
Back knee tracks straight down
Match the reps, not the weight, across sides

exercises.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
joints: rear-leg hip extension at long length
exercises.position: Elevating the rear foot shifts almost all the load to the front leg and takes the hip into deeper flexion, so the glute works at longer length than in a flat split squat. Near-barbell-squat stimulus per leg at a fraction of the spinal load — the workhorse substitute for a back that will not tolerate loaded bilateral squatting.
exercises.resistance: Dumbbells or barbell. Hardest at the bottom, glute loaded in the lengthened position.
cues: Front shin roughly vertical, or let the knee travel for more quad
Do not push off the back foot
Dumbbells at the sides keep the load off the spine

exercises.name: Reverse Lunge
exercises.position: Stepping backward keeps the front knee more stacked than a forward lunge and gives the knee an easier ride, which is why it is usually the lunge of choice for a sensitive knee.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or dumbbells.
cues: Step back and down, not back and out
Front heel stays planted
Stand up through the front leg

exercises.name: Lateral Lunge
exercises.position: Frontal-plane loading with a long adductor stretch on the trailing leg. The strength counterpart to skater hops, and one of very few places the adductors get loaded at length deliberately.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or held load.
cues: Sit into the bent hip, keep the other leg straight
Both feet stay flat and pointing forward
Chest tall

exercises.name: Step-Up
exercises.gct: n/a — dead start from the box
exercises.position: Mostly concentric: you build the rep from a dead start on the box rather than lowering into it. Box height sets hip flexion and therefore how much glute versus quad you get.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or dumbbells.
cues: Drive through the top foot — do not push off the floor
Control the way down or step down
Knee tracks over the foot

exercises.name: Step-Down
exercises.position: The eccentric mirror of the step-up, and a standard knee-rehab progression because the quad is loaded slowly through control rather than output. Same family, opposite contraction emphasis.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, eccentric.
cues: Lower under control — the slow part is the exercise
Tap the heel, do not land on it
Keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Overhead Split Squat
exercises.position: Holding load overhead forces the trunk upright and punishes any rib flare, so the limiting factor becomes trunk and shoulder position rather than leg strength. Light loads, high control demand.
exercises.resistance: External, overhead. Position-limited, not strength-limited.
cues: Ribs down, arms locked
Load stays over the mid-foot
Stop the set when the arms drift forward

exercises.name: Single-Leg RDL
exercises.position: Same hamstring-at-length stimulus as an RDL but with an anti-rotation demand the bilateral version has none of, because the free leg's weight tries to twist the pelvis. Loads are necessarily light, so lumbar flexion stress is much lower than a barbell RDL.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or light held load. Balance-limited before strength-limited.
cues: Hips square — do not let the free hip open
Reach the heel back behind you
Standing knee soft, not locked

exercises.name: Single-Leg Dumbbell RDL
exercises.position: Load hangs from the hands, so the spine is in traction rather than compression — the mechanical opposite of a barbell good morning at a similar hip angle. This is why it survives on a lumbar-limited programme where the barbell hinges do not.
exercises.resistance: External, hanging. Hardest at the bottom.
cues: Let the weight hang — do not row it
Pelvis stays level
Same depth both sides or the set does not count

exercises.name: Staggered RDL
exercises.position: Rear toe touching down removes most of the balance demand while keeping the load unilateral, so you can go heavier than a true single-leg RDL. The bridge between bilateral and single-leg hinging.
exercises.resistance: External. Heavier than a single-leg RDL, lighter than bilateral.
cues: Rear foot is a kickstand, not a second leg
Most of the weight through the lead heel
Hinge, do not squat

exercises.name: Single-Leg Good Morning
exercises.position: Combines the good morning's axial load and long flexion lever with a single-leg balance demand. High skill, high lumbar cost — included to mark the ceiling of this family rather than as a default prescription.
exercises.resistance: External, axial. Light loads only.
cues: Very light — the bar is for position, not load
Hips square throughout
Stop at the first sign of rounding

exercises.name: Nordic Curl
exercises.position: Knee flexion with the hip extended, so the hamstrings work at the knee while short at the hip — the complement to an RDL, which works them at the hip while they stay long at the knee. Prescribing only one of the two leaves half the muscle's function untrained.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, eccentric and brutal. Hardest near full extension.
exercises.dose: 2–3 × 3–6, slow lowering; low volume, high soreness
equipment: partner, or a bar/pad to anchor the feet
cues: Hips stay extended — no hinging to cheat the lever
Lower as slowly as you can, then push back up
Start with a band or a shorter range

exercises.name: Glute Ham Raise
exercises.position: Unlike the Nordic, this trains both of the hamstrings' jobs in one rep — knee flexion and hip extension — which is why it is the closest single exercise to the muscle's actual function in running.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight on the apparatus; can be loaded.
cues: Lead with the knees, finish with the hips
Keep the trunk and thigh in line
Lower under control rather than dropping

exercises.name: Hamstring Curl
exercises.position: Pure knee flexion with no hip involvement, so the hamstrings shorten at the knee while hip position fixes their length. It is not a substitute for an RDL and an RDL is not a substitute for it — the shared label 'hamstrings' hides two different joint actions.
exercises.resistance: Machine or band. Profile depends on the machine; usually hardest mid-range.
cues: Control the return, do not let it snap back
Hips stay down on the pad
Full range both ways

exercises.name: Glute Bridge
exercises.position: Supine, so the spine is supported and there is no axial load or flexion moment at all. Peak tension is at the top, where the glute is shortest — the opposite profile to a Bulgarian split squat. The lowest-cost glute exercise in the block.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight. Hardest at the top.
cues: Drive through the heels, squeeze at the top
Ribs down — do not arch the back to get higher
Hold the top for a beat

exercises.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
exercises.position: Same supported, zero-spinal-cost position as the bilateral bridge, with an added anti-rotation demand on the pelvis. Doubles the per-side load without adding any equipment.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight. Hardest at the top.
cues: Keep the pelvis level — no dropping on the free side
Free leg stays still
Push the heel into the floor

exercises.name: Bench-Supported Glute Bridge
exercises.position: Shoulders on a bench lengthens the range and lets the movement be loaded heavily while the spine stays unloaded in compression terms. The heaviest glute work available to someone who cannot load a barbell on their back.
exercises.resistance: External, across the hips. Hardest at the top.
cues: Chin tucked, ribs down
Finish with the pelvis level, not hyperextended
Full range — do not shorten it to add weight

exercises.name: Hamstring Bridge
exercises.position: Straightening the knees shifts the bridge from glute-dominant to hamstring-dominant, because the hamstrings are now longer at the knee and better placed to extend the hip. Same family, different muscle emphasis from one modifier.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight. Hardest at the top.
cues: Heels on the support, legs long
Lift from the hamstrings, not the lower back
Stop if it cramps — that is the cue to regress

exercises.name: Leg Extension
exercises.position: The one exercise here that trains the rectus femoris properly: seated with the hip flexed it is partly short, but reducing the hip flexion angle lengthens it and raises its contribution markedly. Squats grow the vasti and largely miss the rectus femoris, so this is a complement rather than a redundancy.
exercises.resistance: Machine. Hardest in the mid-to-shortened range on most machines.
cues: Control the lowering
Recline the seat back to bias the rectus femoris
Do not slam into the end range

flags.text: The hip-angle effect is measured: 40° of hip flexion produced significantly more proximal and mid-belly rectus femoris activation than 80°, and the biarticular rectus femoris is subject to active insufficiency when the hip is flexed. Source: Journal of Sports Sciences, hip flexion angle and quadriceps hypertrophy in leg extension.

swap_edges.same: Loaded squat pattern, lengthened-biased, strength and hypertrophy intent
swap_edges.changed: Unilateral, dumbbells instead of a barbell and rack
swap_edges.dose: Per side; load is not a % of squat 1RM — prescribe to effort

swap_edges.same: Barbell bilateral squat, lengthened bias, strength and hypertrophy intent
swap_edges.changed: Upright trunk shortens the hip moment arm, so much less lumbar flexion demand at the same load
Isometric instead of dynamic; no external load

swap_edges.same: Knee-flexion hamstring work with the hip extended
swap_edges.changed: Bodyweight eccentric instead of machine; far harder

swap_edges.same: Hip extension, shortened-position peak, no spinal load
swap_edges.changed: Bodyweight unilateral instead of loaded bilateral

swap_edges.same: Lengthened-biased squat pattern for strength and hypertrophy
swap_edges.changed: Axial load removed — dumbbells hang at the sides instead of a bar on the spine
swap_edges.dose: Per side; prescribe to effort, not % 1RM

swap_edges.changed: Back supported, no load, isometric only

swap_edges.same: Hip-hinge posterior chain work at long hamstring length
swap_edges.changed: Load hangs from the hands rather than sitting on the spine; flexion lever much shorter

swap_edges.same: Posterior chain, hamstring and glute emphasis
swap_edges.changed: No axial load and no long flexion lever
Spine in traction rather than compression; much lighter

swap_edges.same: Hip extension, glute and hamstring emphasis
swap_edges.changed: Supine and supported — no flexion moment at all; peak shifts to the shortened position
Load hangs in front and is far lighter; ballistic rather than grinding
Spine supported and unloaded instead of axially loaded in flexion
Hinge instead of squat — far less knee flexion under load

swap_edges.same: Lower-body isolation with no spinal cost
swap_edges.changed: Hip extension instead of knee extension; removes knee loading entirely
Apparatus assists, and the concentric is achievable
Rear foot on the floor — less load on the front leg, much less balance demand
Rear toe down removes most of the balance demand
Back rack is less demanding on mobility and trunk position
No rack or platform needed
No barbell or platform; balance-limited
